subject: biology
title: Animal systems
summary: How animal cells specialise and organise into tissues, organs and systems, with the structure and function of the mammalian digestive, endocrine and excretory systems and how they work together.
body:
A mammal is made of trillions of cells, but those cells do not all do the same job. Some absorb food, some send chemical messages and some clean the blood. In this lesson you will see how cells specialise and organise into tissues, organs and systems, and how three systems (digestive, endocrine and excretory) each do their own job while also depending on each other.

## Key ideas

### Cell specialisation

Every cell in your body carries the same DNA, yet a nerve cell looks and behaves nothing like a red blood cell. This happens through **cell specialisation** (also called **differentiation**): during development, each cell switches on only some of its genes. The proteins it makes give it a particular shape and set of organelles that suit one job.

Examples of structure matching function:

- Cells lining the small intestine have **microvilli**, tiny folds of the plasma membrane that greatly increase the surface area for absorption. They also have many mitochondria to supply ATP for active transport.
- Cells in the pancreas that make digestive enzymes have lots of rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, because they make and export large amounts of protein.
- Cells in the kidney tubules also have microvilli and many mitochondria, because they actively pump useful substances back into the blood.

### Levels of organisation

Specialised cells are arranged in a hierarchy:

`cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism`

- A **tissue** is a group of similar cells working together on one function.
- An **organ** is a structure made of two or more tissue types working together (for example, the stomach).
- An **organ system** is a group of organs that work together to carry out a major function (for example, the digestive system).

Animals have four main tissue types:

| Tissue | What it is like | Main role | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Epithelial** | Sheets of tightly packed cells | Covers surfaces and lines tubes; absorbs and secretes | Lining of the small intestine |
| **Connective** | Cells spread through a matrix | Supports, binds and transports | Blood, bone, cartilage |
| **Muscle** | Cells that can contract | Movement | Smooth muscle in the gut wall |
| **Nervous** | Neurons and support cells | Carries electrical signals | Nerves controlling gut movement |

The stomach is a good example of an organ: epithelial tissue lines it and secretes acid and enzymes, smooth muscle churns the food, connective tissue holds it together and carries blood vessels, and nervous tissue coordinates it all.

### The digestive system

The **digestive system** breaks large food molecules into small ones that can be absorbed into the blood. **Mechanical digestion** physically breaks food into smaller pieces (chewing, churning). **Chemical digestion** uses enzymes to break chemical bonds, turning large molecules into small ones.

| Part | What happens |
|---|---|
| Mouth | Teeth chew food (mechanical). Saliva contains **amylase**, which starts breaking starch into sugars. |
| Oesophagus | Moves food to the stomach by **peristalsis**, waves of smooth muscle contraction. No digestion here. |
| Stomach | Churns food. Hydrochloric acid kills many microbes and gives the low pH that **pepsin** needs to begin protein digestion. |
| Small intestine | Most chemical digestion and nearly all nutrient absorption. Enzymes from the pancreas and the intestinal lining finish digesting carbohydrates, proteins and lipids. |
| Large intestine | Absorbs water and some ions; forms faeces. |
| Rectum and anus | Stores and then removes faeces (egestion). |

Two **accessory organs** help but food never passes through them:

- The **liver** makes **bile**, which is stored in the gall bladder. Bile is not an enzyme. It **emulsifies** fats, breaking large fat droplets into tiny droplets so lipase has much more surface area to act on.
- The **pancreas** releases pancreatic juice into the small intestine. It contains amylase, proteases and lipase, plus bicarbonate to neutralise acid arriving from the stomach.

The small intestine is built for absorption. Its inner wall is folded, the folds are covered in finger-like **villi**, and each epithelial cell has microvilli. This gives an enormous surface area. Each villus has a thin epithelium, a network of blood capillaries (which take up sugars and amino acids) and a **lacteal**, a lymph vessel that takes up digested fats.

### The endocrine system

The **endocrine system** is made of **glands** that secrete **hormones**, chemical messengers released straight into the blood. Hormones travel throughout the body, but only **target cells** respond, because only they have the matching **receptor** proteins.

| Gland | Example hormone | Main effect |
|---|---|---|
| Hypothalamus (brain) | Releasing hormones; makes ADH | Controls the pituitary; links nervous and endocrine systems |
| Pituitary | TSH; releases ADH | Controls other glands; ADH controls water reabsorption in kidneys |
| Thyroid | Thyroxine | Sets metabolic rate |
| Pancreas (islets) | Insulin, glucagon | Controls blood glucose |
| Adrenal glands | Adrenaline | Prepares the body for action |

Compared with nerve signals, hormone responses are usually slower to start but last longer and can affect many tissues at once.

### The excretory system

**Excretion** is the removal of **metabolic wastes**, substances made by the body's own chemical reactions. (Removing undigested food as faeces is egestion, not excretion.) A key waste is **urea**. When the body has more amino acids than it needs, the liver removes their nitrogen-containing amino groups (**deamination**). This forms toxic ammonia, which the liver quickly converts to less toxic urea.

The mammalian **excretory system** (urinary system) includes two **kidneys**, two **ureters**, the **bladder** and the **urethra**. Each kidney contains about a million **nephrons**, the tiny tubules that make urine:

1. **Filtration**: high blood pressure in a knot of capillaries called the **glomerulus** pushes water and small molecules (glucose, salts, urea, amino acids) into **Bowman's capsule**. Blood cells and large proteins are too big and stay in the blood. The fluid is now called **filtrate**.
2. **Selective reabsorption**: in the tubule, useful substances move back into the blood. All glucose and amino acids are normally reabsorbed (largely by active transport), as is most of the water and salt.
3. **Secretion**: some substances, such as certain ions and drugs, are actively moved from the blood into the tubule.
4. Urine passes through the collecting ducts to the ureters, is stored in the bladder and leaves through the urethra.

How much water is reabsorbed in the collecting duct is controlled by the hormone ADH (covered in the homeostasis lesson).

### How the systems connect

No system works alone; the **circulatory system** links them all.

- The digestive system absorbs amino acids. Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver, and the urea produced travels in the blood to the kidneys to be excreted.
- The pancreas belongs to two systems: it releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine and secretes insulin and glucagon into the blood.
- Absorbed glucose raises blood glucose, which the endocrine system then regulates.
- The endocrine system controls the excretory system: ADH changes how much water the kidneys keep.
- Hormones made by the gut itself help coordinate digestion, for example by triggering release of pancreatic juice when acidic food enters the small intestine.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: a blocked bile duct

A gallstone blocks the duct carrying bile to the small intestine. Predict the effect on digestion.

1. Identify bile's role: it emulsifies fats; it does not digest them.
2. Without bile, fats stay as large droplets with a small surface area.
3. Lipase can only act on the surface of droplets, so fat digestion becomes much slower.
4. Less fat is digested and absorbed, so more fat passes into the faeces.
5. Carbohydrate and protein digestion are mostly unaffected, because their enzymes come from the pancreas and gut lining.

### Example 2: interpreting kidney data

A table gives concentrations in a healthy person (g per 100 mL):

| Substance | Blood plasma | Filtrate | Urine |
|---|---|---|---|
| Protein | 8.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| Glucose | 0.1 | 0.1 | 0.0 |
| Urea | 0.03 | 0.03 | 2.0 |

1. Protein: in plasma but not filtrate, so it is too large to pass through the glomerulus.
2. Glucose: same in plasma and filtrate, so it is filtered freely; it is absent from urine, so it is completely reabsorbed.
3. Urea: much more concentrated in urine than filtrate. Urea is not reabsorbed as much as water is, so as water is taken back into the blood, the urea left behind becomes concentrated.

## Common mistakes

- Saying bile digests fat. Bile emulsifies; lipase digests.
- Calling the removal of faeces excretion. Faeces are mostly undigested food that was never part of body cells, so this is egestion.
- Thinking urea is made in the kidneys. It is made in the liver and only removed by the kidneys.
- Saying hormones act on every cell they reach. Only cells with the matching receptor respond.
- Mixing up villi (multicellular projections of the gut wall) with microvilli (folds of a single cell's membrane).

## Exam tips

- When asked how a structure suits its function, name the feature AND explain the link (for example: villi increase surface area, so more nutrients are absorbed per unit time).
- Be ready to place structures on a hierarchy: a nephron is part of an organ (kidney), which is part of a system.
- Data questions on plasma, filtrate and urine are common. Compare columns in pairs and say what each comparison tells you.
- For questions about interactions between systems, trace one substance (such as an amino acid) through each system in order.

## Tips to remember

- **"Every Cat Needs Milk"** for the four animal tissues: **E**pithelial, **C**onnective, **N**ervous, **M**uscle. (A made-up memory trick.)
- **Bile breaks, lipase takes**: bile only emulsifies big fat droplets into tiny ones; lipase is the enzyme that actually digests the fat. (A made-up memory trick.)
- **Excretion vs egestion**: **ex**cretion removes what the body **made** (like urea); **eg**estion removes what you **ate** but never absorbed (faeces).
- **Nephron in three verbs: Filter, Fetch back, Flush out**: filtration at the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule, selective reabsorption of useful substances (all glucose and amino acids, most water and salt), then secretion of some ions and drugs from the blood into the tubule. (A made-up memory trick.)
- **Hormones are like a radio broadcast**: the signal reaches every cell in the blood, but only target cells "tuned in" with the matching receptor respond.
- **Liver makes, kidney takes**: urea is made in the liver by deamination, then carried in the blood to the kidneys to be excreted.

## Key terms

- **Cell specialisation** — the process by which cells develop a particular structure suited to a particular function
- **Tissue** — a group of similar cells working together to perform a function
- **Organ** — a structure made of several tissue types working together
- **Organ system** — a group of organs working together to carry out a major function
- **Mechanical digestion** — physical breakdown of food into smaller pieces
- **Chemical digestion** — enzyme breakdown of large food molecules into smaller ones
- **Peristalsis** — waves of smooth muscle contraction that push food along the gut
- **Villi** — finger-like projections of the small intestine wall that increase surface area for absorption
- **Emulsification** — breaking large fat droplets into smaller droplets
- **Hormone** — a chemical messenger secreted into the blood by an endocrine gland
- **Target cell** — a cell with receptors for a particular hormone
- **Excretion** — removal of metabolic wastes made by the body
- **Deamination** — removal of the amino group from an amino acid, forming ammonia and then urea
- **Nephron** — the functional unit of the kidney that filters blood and forms urine
- **Glomerulus** — the knot of capillaries where blood is filtered into Bowman's capsule

## Summary

- Specialised cells form tissues, organs and organ systems; structure always matches function.
- The digestive system breaks food down mechanically and chemically; the small intestine, with its villi and microvilli, absorbs nutrients.
- The endocrine system uses hormones carried in the blood to act on target cells with matching receptors.
- The kidneys excrete urea through filtration, selective reabsorption and secretion in nephrons.
- Systems are linked by the blood: the liver makes urea from absorbed amino acids, the pancreas serves both digestion and hormone control, and ADH controls kidney water reabsorption.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an organ?

options.A: A group of identical cells performing the same function
options.B: A group of organ systems working together
options.C: A single specialised cell with many organelles
options.D: A structure made of two or more tissue types working together

questions.explanation: An organ, such as the stomach, contains several tissue types (epithelial, muscle, connective, nervous) working together. Option A describes a tissue, which is the level just below an organ and a common mix-up.

questions.prompt: What is the role of bile in digestion?

options.A: It emulsifies fats, increasing the surface area for lipase
options.B: It chemically breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol
options.C: It begins protein digestion in the stomach
options.D: It absorbs digested fats into the lacteals

questions.explanation: Bile physically breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones, giving lipase more surface to act on. It contains no digestive enzymes, so B (which describes lipase) is wrong even though it is tempting.

questions.prompt: Cells lining the kidney tubules have many microvilli and many mitochondria. The best explanation is that these cells

options.C: reabsorb substances, often by active transport, across a large surface area
options.D: secrete hormones directly into the blood

questions.explanation: Microvilli increase surface area and mitochondria supply ATP for active transport, which suits reabsorption of glucose and other substances. Filtration (A) happens at the glomerulus and is driven by blood pressure, not ATP from tubule cells.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of excretion?

options.A: Removal of undigested fibre in faeces
options.C: Release of insulin into the blood
options.D: Release of bile into the small intestine

questions.explanation: Urea is a metabolic waste made by the liver from excess amino acids, so removing it is excretion. Fibre (A) was never part of body cells' metabolism, so its removal is egestion, a very common confusion.

questions.prompt: Why can insulin travel through the whole bloodstream but only affect some cells?

options.A: Insulin is broken down before it reaches most cells
options.C: Insulin can only enter cells by active transport
options.D: Only target cells have receptors that bind insulin

questions.explanation: Hormones reach almost every cell, but only cells with the matching receptor respond. Option A is tempting because hormones are eventually broken down, but that is not why responses are limited to particular cells.

questions.prompt: A person eats a meal high in protein. Which sequence correctly traces excess nitrogen from the food to its removal from the body?

options.A: Small intestine absorbs amino acids → liver deaminates them to form urea → blood carries urea → kidneys excrete urea
options.B: Stomach makes urea → small intestine absorbs urea → kidneys excrete urea
options.C: Small intestine absorbs amino acids → kidneys convert them to urea → bladder stores urea
options.D: Large intestine absorbs amino acids → pancreas converts them to urea → liver excretes urea

questions.explanation: Amino acids are absorbed in the small intestine, the liver deaminates excess amino acids and converts the ammonia to urea, and the kidneys remove urea from the blood. Option C is tempting because the kidneys handle urea, but they do not make it.

questions.prompt: In a healthy person, glucose is present in the filtrate in Bowman's capsule but absent from urine. This shows that glucose is

options.A: too large to pass through the glomerulus
options.B: filtered and then completely reabsorbed into the blood
options.C: secreted into the tubule from the blood
options.D: converted to urea in the nephron

questions.explanation: Glucose appears in the filtrate, so it is filtered; it is missing from urine, so all of it must be reabsorbed. Option A cannot be right because a molecule too large to be filtered would not appear in the filtrate at all (like plasma proteins).

questions.prompt: A disease damages the villi of the small intestine so that they become flattened. Which outcome is most likely?

options.A: Starch digestion in the mouth stops
options.C: Less nutrient absorption, because the absorptive surface area is reduced
options.D: More water is absorbed in the small intestine, causing dehydration

questions.explanation: Villi greatly increase the surface area of the small intestine. Flattened villi mean less surface for absorption, so fewer nutrients enter the blood. Bile (B) is made in the liver, so damage to the intestine lining would not stop its production.
